docs.text: Configuring an analysis Start from the supplied template and adjust it to your experiment. Shared settings describe your inputs and analysis; the named blocks hold settings for each analysis step. The pipeline reference lists the available parameters and their effective defaults. Create a run configuration Keep the pipeline installation separate from the analysis directory: mkdir -p /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort cp /path/to/SpectroMesa-DDA/config/template.config \ /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort/run.config Edit the copied file. Keep its includeConfig statements and final methods.setup() call. Nextflow's projectDir points to the pipeline installation when you launch its main.nf , so those statements still work from your analysis directory. Add all parameter changes before methods.setup() . The required shared settings are: params { input_csv = '/project/analyses/human_dda_cohort/acquisitions.csv' decoy_database = '/data/databases/human-decoy_contam.fasta' msfragger_executable = '/opt/MSFragger/MSFragger-4.4.1.jar' output_dir = '/project/results' dataset_id = 'human_dda_cohort' experiment_type = 'LFQ' contam_string = 'CONTAM_' } These are fragments to edit into your copied template, not replacements for the whole file. Use your actual paths and the contaminant marker in your FASTA. dataset_id defaults to cohort ; choose a meaningful name without spaces. The MSFragger JAR is required only when that engine is selected. Select LFQ or TMT experiment_type already defaults to LFQ . For TMT, change it to TMT and provide the channel manifest: params { experiment_type = 'TMT' channel_csv = '/project/analyses/human_dda_cohort/channels.csv' quantitate_ProteomicTMT { plex_type = 'tmt10plex' } } The pipeline detects fractionation from your acquisition CSV . Keep the sample/plex identifiers and fraction layout consistent; no separate fractionation switch is needed. Database searching Choose search engines MSFragger is already selected by default. To use Sage alone, or combine search engines, edit search_engines : params { search_ProteomicMSMS { search_engines = ['MSFragger', 'Comet', 'Sage'] } } Use any nonempty combination of those three names without duplicates. Multiple engines increase runtime and storage use. Their identifications are combined automatically during validation; you do not need to enable consensus merging separately. Mass tolerances Match tolerances to your instrument, acquisition, and calibration. Each search engine has its own block. For example, these are MSFragger's current template values: params { search_ProteomicMSMS { MSFraggerAdapter { tolerance { precursor_mass_tolerance_lower = 30.0 precursor_mass_tolerance_upper = 30.0 precursor_mass_unit = 'ppm' fragment_mass_tolerance = 0.02 fragment_mass_unit = 'Da' } } } } The two precursor settings describe the lower and upper tolerance widths. Sage uses signed left/right bounds instead. See Database search for each engine's parameter names and values. Digestion and modifications Set the enzyme and modifications to match sample preparation for every selected engine . MSFragger's default template uses trypsin with two missed cleavages and carbamidomethylated cysteine. It also includes variable methionine oxidation, protein N-terminal acetylation, and N-terminal glutamine cyclization. Comet and Sage have their own modification lists, so review them when combining engines. For a different digestion enzyme, change the search settings and validate_ProteomicPSM.enzyme together. The validation default is Trypsin . TMT reporter settings do not configure search modifications Setting experiment_type = 'TMT' or plex_type does not add TMT labels to the search. Configure the correct label mass on lysine and peptide N termini for each engine you use. For conventional TMT10 labeling with MSFragger, the integration example uses: params { search_ProteomicMSMS { MSFraggerAdapter { statmod { add_C_cysteine = 57.021464 add_K_lysine = 229.162932 add_nterm_peptide = 229.162932 } } } } Use the mass appropriate to your actual reagent; TMTpro uses different chemistry. Review variable modifications too, especially when a fixed label changes which modifications can occur at the same site. Spectrum identifiers reindex_mzml defaults to false in SpectroMesa-DDA. Enable search_ProteomicMSMS.reindex_mzml = true when you need unique native spectrum IDs across a sample's fractions. The resulting mzML files are passed consistently to validation, quantitation, and QC. This option is covered by a TMT integration case. Identification validation Percolator rescoring is already enabled. The default percolator_workflow = 'openms' uses the OpenMS adapter. To add prediction-based features with MSBooster, set: params { validate_ProteomicPSM { percolator_workflow = 'msbooster' } } filter_psm_score_peptide already defaults to 0.01 . Despite its historical name, this is a PSM q-value cutoff for the filtered identification output. It is not a protein FDR threshold. Keep run_percolator = true for the default ProteinProphet grouping route, which uses the unfiltered PEP-scored results. LFQ quantitation LFQ already uses the identification-guided FFId route. merge_featureXML is enabled so the pipeline produces the combined feature map required for protein quantitation; keep it enabled for an end-to-end run. save_intermediate_files is true in the LFQ template launched by SpectroMesa-DDA . Set quantitate_ProteomicLFQ.save_intermediate_files = false if you do not need the published intermediate feature maps; final results and execution logs remain available. Match between runs is off by default . If appropriate for your experiment, enable quantitate_ProteomicLFQ.enable_mbr = true . It requires at least two samples and merge_featureXML = true . This transfers identification evidence between linked features and changes how missing identifications are handled. Review the LFQ reference before enabling it. TMT quantitation The default tmt_workflow = 'scan_based' quantifies reporter ions. Normalization is already enabled, and the template launched by SpectroMesa-DDA selects tmt_normalization_method = 'mad' . Label one channel in each plex reference in the channel CSV , unless you deliberately enable a virtual reference. MAD produces reference-scaled quasi-intensities by default. For scan-based quantitation, you can instead choose tmt_normalization_method = 'openms' to use IsobaricAnalyzer's median-ratio normalization with a physical reference. MADNormalizer.quasi_intensity = false instead produces log2 ratios, changing the meaning of the output values. Disable normalization altogether with enable_tmt_normalization = false if that is your intended analysis. Feature-based TMT is experimental The optional feature_based route apportions integrated MS1 feature areas using reporter-ion proportions. It requires matching fraction IDs across plexes. When normalization is enabled, keep mad ; switching to openms normalization is incompatible with this route. Validate its behavior on representative data before using it for biological comparisons. The TMT reference explains virtual references, bridge scaling, isotope correction, and the two workflows. Protein grouping and quantitation quantitate_ProteomicProtein.protein_grouping_algorithm already defaults to ProteinProphet . This combines the unfiltered PEP-scored identifications across the cohort with iProphet and ProteinProphet, then quantifies the resulting groups with OpenMS ProteinQuantifier. The protein cutoff is not enabled automatically protein_fdr_cutoff defaults to 0.01 , but filter_protein_fdr and protein_inference_protein_fdr both default to false . The default ProteinProphet route removes zero-probability groups; it does not apply a 1% protein q-value filter. Do not describe its output as filtered to 1% protein FDR. The alternative ProteinInferencer route can calculate and filter protein FDR when both switches are enabled: params { quantitate_ProteomicProtein { protein_grouping_algorithm = 'ProteinInferencer' protein_inference_protein_fdr = true filter_protein_fdr = true protein_fdr_cutoff = 0.01 } } ProteinQuantifier combines charge states by default ( protein_quantifier_best_charge = false ) and sums fractions within each assay ( protein_quantifier_fractions_aggregate = 'sum' ). See the protein reference before changing these choices. Computing resources Choose a container profile, normally docker or apptainer , when launching. The bundled resource plans are: Resource profile Node budget boutroslab_aws 32 CPUs, 128 GB pines 64 CPUs, 500 GB Combine the resource plan and runtime, for example -profile pines,apptainer . These plans control local task allocations; they do not request a Slurm job. Launch inside an allocation of the matching size. For a custom machine, copy a JSON plan from config/resource_profiles/ into a directory you control, rename it my_cluster.json , and adjust its CPU/memory budget and process requests. Keep every pipeline and process entry. Then set: params { compute_profile = 'my_cluster' additional_resource_profile_dir = '/project/resource_profiles' } The custom directory is searched before bundled profiles. Multiple directories may be separated by : on Linux/macOS. A corresponding Nextflow -profile my_cluster is not needed. See Shared parameters for per-step limits and allocation adjustments. Results database ProteoVault assembly is already enabled with run_proteovault = true . Leave it enabled to create the DuckDB database for analysis with ProteoVaultR . Set it to false to finish after QC while retaining the individual result files. Next, follow Running and resuming to launch from your analysis directory.

docs.text: Running and resuming an analysis Once you have installed SpectroMesa-DDA , prepared your inputs , and created a run configuration , you can launch the analysis with Nextflow. Start with a small representative subset of your data to check the setup before processing the full cohort. Choose a work directory Nextflow stores intermediate files in a work directory, separate from the results directory specified by output_dir . Choose a location with enough space and keep it available until you have finished the analysis and no longer need to resume it. Use the same work path each time you launch or resume this analysis. In the examples below, replace /scratch/your_user/human_dda_cohort/work with a suitable location on your system. All machines running the analysis must be able to access it. Keep a stable work path between jobs Avoid using $SLURM_JOB_ID in the work path if you want to resume across cluster jobs: each job has a different ID. Also check your site's scratch retention policy. A stable path is only useful for resuming while its contents remain available. Storage use depends on conversion, the number of search engines, fractionation, and feature extraction. Keep space for the input data, intermediate files, published results, and container images. Measure peak usage on a representative pilot run before sizing a full cohort; there is no measured DDA-specific storage multiplier for this pipeline. Start an analysis On a workstation Use a dedicated directory for each analysis, such as /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort . Keep your prepared run.config there and launch Nextflow from that directory. Nextflow stores its run history and .nextflow.log there, while the pipeline itself can remain in a separate installation directory: cd /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DDA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort/run.config \ -profile docker \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dda_cohort/work Replace the example paths with your own. This example uses Docker; choose apptainer if that is what you installed. Review the computing resource settings to make sure the analysis fits your workstation. Keep the terminal session running until Nextflow finishes. -c selects your run configuration, -profile selects the execution environment, and -work-dir sets the intermediate-file location. The results still go to the output_dir in your configuration. On a Slurm cluster Run the analysis inside a compute allocation. For example, the following submission script requests resources matching the bundled boutroslab_aws resource profile and uses Apptainer. That profile can be used on a suitably sized node; its name does not require an AWS environment. Save this as run-dda.sh in your analysis directory, replace the paths, and adjust the time limit and any partition or account settings required by your cluster: #!/usr/bin/env bash #SBATCH --job-name=human_dda #SBATCH --nodes=1 #SBATCH --ntasks=1 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=32 #SBATCH --mem=128G #SBATCH --time=24:00:00 #SBATCH --output=human_dda-%j.log set -euo pipefail # Load Java, Nextflow, and Apptainer here if your cluster uses modules. cd /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DDA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort/run.config \ -profile boutroslab_aws,apptainer \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dda_cohort/work Submit it from the same analysis directory: cd /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort sbatch run-dda.sh The 24-hour limit is an example, not an expected runtime. Choose an appropriate limit for your cohort and cluster. The profile sets CPU and memory use; sbatch requests the allocation. For a different allocation, use a matching custom resource profile . Keep container images available between runs For Apptainer, use persistent image caches as described in Installation . Export those cache settings in your submission script as well. This avoids downloading and converting the same images repeatedly. Monitor progress Nextflow prints progress and any errors to the terminal. For the Slurm example, this output is saved to human_dda-<job-id>.log in the directory from which you submitted the script. The launch directory also contains .nextflow.log with more detailed messages. A stage such as searching or quantitation may take a long time without changing the top-level progress display. Check its logs before assuming that the analysis has stopped. The pipeline writes execution reports under: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DDA-<version>/<dataset_id>/ log-SpectroMesa-DDA-<version>-<timestamp>/nextflow-log/ trace.txt timeline.html report.html The HTML reports are most useful after the run finishes. They summarize task execution, timing, and resource use. Analysis stages also save their own logs alongside their outputs. A successful run exits with status 0 and has no failed tasks. On a cluster, check the job's final status as well as the Nextflow log. The presence of some result files alone does not mean the whole analysis completed successfully, because results are written as stages finish. If the run fails, read the reported error and the failed task's .command.err and .command.out files in the work directory shown by Nextflow. Correct the cause before trying to resume. Resume an interrupted run Add -resume to the original command, using the same launch directory, configuration, profiles, and work path. For the workstation example: cd /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DDA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort/run.config \ -profile docker \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dda_cohort/work \ -resume For the Slurm example, add -resume to the Nextflow command in run-dda.sh and submit the script again after the previous job has stopped. An interrupted stage starts again Resume currently works at the level of completed analysis stages. Nextflow can reuse a completed stage when its cached results are available and its inputs and settings still match. Work completed inside an unfinished stage is not automatically resumed. For example, if searching stops halfway through the cohort, expect the search stage to run again; completed earlier stages may be reused. Return to the same analysis directory when resuming, and keep its .nextflow folder and the original work directory. Published results alone are not enough to resume. Changing inputs, settings, or pipeline code can cause affected stages to run again. See Nextflow's resume documentation for the cache requirements. Plain -resume selects the most recent run. If you have launched another analysis from the same directory, list previous runs with: nextflow log Then use -resume RUN_NAME , replacing RUN_NAME with the name of the intended run. Do not start two attempts to resume the same run at once. Find your results The main analysis outputs are under: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DDA-<version>/<dataset_id>/main_workflow/ Look for the versioned quantitate-ProteomicProtein-* directory for final protein and peptide abundance tables, and qc-ProteomicDDA-* for QC summaries and plots. The results guide explains LFQ sample columns and TMT channel columns. ProteoVault database assembly is enabled by default. When generated, the database is published one level above the dataset directory: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DDA-<version>/<dataset_id>.proteovault.duckdb You can load the generated DuckDB database into R and analyze the results using ProteoVaultR . Keep the run configuration and logs with your results. Once the analysis is complete, review the QC summaries before interpreting the quantitative comparisons. Retain the work directory if you expect to resume or investigate individual analysis steps.

For the workstation example: cd /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DDA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dda_cohort/run.config \ -profile docker \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dda_cohort/work \ -resume For the Slurm example, add -resume to the Nextflow command in run-dda.sh and submit the script again after the previous job has stopped. An interrupted stage starts again Resume currently works at the level of completed analysis stages. Nextflow can reuse a completed stage when its cached results are available and its inputs and settings still match. Work completed inside an unfinished stage is not automatically resumed. For example, if searching stops halfway through the cohort, expect the search stage to run again; completed earlier stages may be reused. Changing inputs, settings, or pipeline code can cause affected stages to run again. See Nextflow's resume documentation for the cache requirements. Plain -resume selects the most recent run. If you have launched another analysis from the same directory, list previous runs with: nextflow log Then use -resume RUN_NAME , replacing RUN_NAME with the name of the intended run. docs.text: Preparing inputs An LFQ analysis needs two inputs : an acquisition CSV pointing to your mass spectrometry files, and a target-decoy protein FASTA. A TMT analysis needs those same inputs plus a channel CSV describing the samples in each plex. The acquisition files are part of the first input: a CSV pointing to missing files is not a valid input. The separately obtained MSFragger JAR is part of installation , rather than a sample input. Acquisition CSV Create one row for each acquisition. Use these columns: Column What to enter sample_name For LFQ, the sample identifier. For TMT, the plex identifier, matching plex_id in the channel CSV. Repeat the name only for fractions belonging to that same sample or plex. fraction_id Fraction identifier, such as 1 , 2 , or F1 . Use 1 for an unfractionated sample. Each sample/fraction pair must be unique. annotation_id Usually the species name, such as human , mouse , or ecoli . Please include it even though the workflows described here do not currently use it. Keep it consistent across a sample's fractions. path Path to an existing mzML or supported vendor acquisition file. Relative paths are resolved from the CSV's directory. scan For WIFF conversion, the path to its existing .wiff.scan companion. Omit this column for mzML input. Give technical replicates distinct names Files with the same sample_name are treated as one sample or TMT plex. Their search results are combined before sample-level validation. Give separate LFQ technical replicates unique names so they remain separate quantitative assays. For TMT, biological samples are identified by their reporter channels, not by the acquisition CSV's sample_name . LFQ samples and fractions An unfractionated LFQ input can look like this: sample_name,fraction_id,annotation_id,path sample_01_rep1,1,human,/data/sample_01_rep1.mzML sample_01_rep2,1,human,/data/sample_01_rep2.mzML For fractionated LFQ, repeat each sample name for its fractions: sample_name,fraction_id,annotation_id,path sample_01,F1,human,/data/sample_01_F1.mzML sample_01,F2,human,/data/sample_01_F2.mzML sample_02,F1,human,/data/sample_02_F1.mzML sample_02,F2,human,/data/sample_02_F2.mzML All LFQ samples must have the same set of fraction IDs , including unfractionated runs. Corresponding fractions are aligned and linked across samples. The pipeline detects fractionation from this table; you do not need to enable it separately. TMT plexes and fractions For TMT, use a plex name in sample_name . Each row still represents one acquisition, not one reporter channel: sample_name,fraction_id,annotation_id,path plex_01,F1,human,/data/plex_01_F1.mzML plex_01,F2,human,/data/plex_01_F2.mzML plex_02,F1,human,/data/plex_02_F1.mzML plex_02,F2,human,/data/plex_02_F2.mzML Every sample or plex must have multiple fractions, or every one must have a single fraction; mixed layouts are rejected. For feature-based TMT, every plex must also have the same set of fraction IDs. The default scan-based TMT route does not require identical fraction sets across plexes. Acquisition paths and naming All rows must use the same file extension; do not mix RAW and mzML files in one run. Existing mzML files go directly to searching. Other supported file formats pass through conversion . Thermo RAW is covered by an integration case; conversion of another format also depends on support in the configured converter and container. The current DDA input reader accepts files, not Bruker .d acquisition directories. Use sample and fraction identifiers beginning with a letter or digit and containing only letters, digits, dots, underscores, or hyphens. Acquisition basenames must not contain additional dots: sample_01_F1.mzML is suitable, while sample.01.F1.mzML is not. mzML filenames must be unique within each sample, and the same acquisition path must not appear twice. Avoid commas in paths. For WIFF conversion, supply its scan companion: sample_name,fraction_id,annotation_id,path,scan sample_01,1,human,/data/sample_01.wiff,/data/sample_01.wiff.scan Keep the acquisition files accessible throughout the run. A path that exists on your laptop but is unavailable on the compute node or inside the container will not work. Protein sequence database Choose a reference proteome For a typical experiment, start with the gene-centric UniProt reference proteome for the species you are studying. Use the canonical protein FASTA. For human and mouse, expect about 20,000 proteins before adding contaminants and decoys. UniProt distributes additional isoform sequences separately in files ending in _additional.fasta.gz . See the UniProt reference proteome file descriptions . Species Reference proteome Canonical protein FASTA Human UP000005640 UP000005640_9606.fasta.gz Mouse UP000000589 UP000000589_10090.fasta.gz For example, download and decompress the human reference proteome: curl -fL -o UP000005640_9606.fasta.gz \ https://ftp.uniprot.org/pub/databases/uniprot/current_release/knowledgebase/reference_proteomes/Eukaryota/UP000005640/UP000005640_9606.fasta.gz gunzip UP000005640_9606.fasta.gz Keep a record of the UniProt release and download date so you can identify the exact database used in your analysis. Choose or extend the target sequence set to match your experiment if it includes multiple species or proteins absent from the reference proteome. Add contaminants and generate decoys The pipeline requires a combined target-decoy FASTA , containing both the proteins you want to identify and decoy sequences used to estimate false discoveries. We also recommend adding common contaminant sequences so that peptides from laboratory contaminants can be assigned to those proteins. MSPtools can prepare this database in one step. No separate cRAP download needed MSPtools bundles the cRAP contaminant sequences. Use --include-crap to add them and generate their decoys along with the reference-protein decoys. After installing MSPtools, run: msptools FASTA CreateDecoyDatabase \ --input-path UP000005640_9606.fasta \ --output-path UP000005640_9606-decoy_contam.fasta \ --include-crap \ --decoy-prefix DECOY_ \ --contam-prefix CONTAM_ Start from a target-only FASTA. The resulting UP000005640_9606-decoy_contam.fasta contains the reference proteins, contaminants, and decoys for both. By default, MSPtools reverses protein sequences while preserving an initial methionine. The command shows its default prefixes, DECOY_ and CONTAM_ , explicitly. The pipeline defaults to CONTAMINANT_ for contaminants, so update that setting as shown below. Match the database markers in your run configuration Set decoy_database to the generated FASTA and check all four marker settings. For the command above, keep the default decoy_string , decoy_position , and contam_position , and change contam_string to CONTAM_ . The matching configuration is: params { decoy_database = '/path/to/UP000005640_9606-decoy_contam.fasta' decoy_string = 'DECOY_' decoy_position = 'prefix' contam_string = 'CONTAM_' contam_position = 'prefix' } Setting Meaning decoy_string The text marking decoy accessions, such as DECOY_ . decoy_position Where the decoy marker occurs. The current MSFragger workflow requires prefix . contam_string The text marking contaminant accessions. The pipeline defaults to CONTAMINANT_ ; use CONTAM_ for the example above. contam_position Where the contaminant marker occurs: prefix or suffix . Use prefix for the MSPtools command above. Match the markers in your FASTA These settings must match the markers in your FASTA accessions. A prefix appears at the beginning of the accession; a suffix appears at the end. With the example above, a contaminant accession begins with CONTAM_ , and its decoy begins with DECOY_CONTAM_ . Changing a pipeline setting does not rewrite the FASTA headers. Edit the matching settings in your copy of the pipeline's template, keeping its existing includeConfig statements and final methods.setup() call. TMT channel CSV For TMT, create a second CSV with plex_id,channel,description . plex_id must match the acquisition CSV's sample_name values exactly. channel is the reporter label, and description identifies the biological sample or technical replicate assigned to that channel. For example, a complete ten-channel plex is: plex_id,channel,description plex_01,126,reference plex_01,127N,sample_01 plex_01,127C,sample_02 plex_01,128N,sample_03 plex_01,128C,sample_04 plex_01,129N,sample_05 plex_01,129C,sample_06 plex_01,130N,sample_07 plex_01,130C,sample_08 plex_01,131,sample_09 Add the corresponding rows for every other plex in the acquisition CSV. Match the labels to quantitate_ProteomicTMT.plex_type , which defaults to tmt10plex ; do not mix reporter types in one analysis. Use distinct descriptions for technical replicates you want to distinguish. Identify the normalization reference With the default MAD normalization and a physical reference, label exactly one channel per plex reference . The alternative OpenMS normalization uses the same channel convention. MAD's optional virtual-reference mode does not need a channel named reference . Choose the route in Configuring an analysis . Before you run Check that every acquisition and required scan companion exists and is accessible on the analysis machine. Check sample/fraction uniqueness and matching fraction sets where required. Set input_csv and decoy_database to the prepared files and match the FASTA accession markers. For TMT, set channel_csv , check every plex and reporter label, and configure the labeling modifications used in the search.

docs.text: Installing SpectroMesa-DDA Requirements SpectroMesa-DDA can be run on a Linux workstation or a cluster compute node with an x86-64 processor. Before you begin, make sure you can access your mass spectrometry data and protein sequence database from that machine, and reserve working storage for the files the pipeline creates along the way. Measure storage use in a pilot run before sizing a large cohort. Install or load the following on the machine that launches the pipeline: Software Requirement Nextflow 24.10.6 with the v1 syntax parser is recommended. See below for selecting the version and parser. Container runtime Docker or Apptainer. Choose the runtime available on your workstation or cluster. Most analysis tools, including OpenMS, Comet, Sage, MSBooster, Percolator, and ProteoVault, are supplied through the configured container images. MSFragger must be obtained separately when you select it as a search engine. Comet-only and Sage-only runs do not need its JAR. Set up Nextflow We recommend Nextflow 24.10.6 . If you already have a newer Nextflow launcher installed, you can select the recommended version and syntax parser with these environment variables: export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 NXF_VER selects the Nextflow version, and NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER selects its syntax parser. To use a newer version, set NXF_VER to that release and keep NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 , provided the release still supports the v1 parser. Version 24.10.6 remains our tested recommendation. Nextflow 24.10.6 requires a compatible Java installation (Java 17–23); Java 17 or 21 is a suitable choice. If Nextflow is not installed, use the official launcher . For a user-local installation, run the following with the environment settings above already exported: mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" curl -fsSL https://get.nextflow.io -o "$HOME/.local/bin/nextflow" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/nextflow" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" nextflow -version Get the pipeline Download a release (recommended) The easiest way to get started is to download the latest release with all submodules . To download the latest release from a terminal, use either wget : wget -O source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/SpectroMesa-DDA/releases/latest/download/source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz or curl : curl -fL -o source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/SpectroMesa-DDA/releases/latest/download/source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz From the directory containing your download, extract it into a folder for the pipeline: mkdir -p SpectroMesa-DDA tar -xzf source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz -C SpectroMesa-DDA --strip-components=1 cd SpectroMesa-DDA You can now continue to check the container runtime . Clone with Git (alternative) If you prefer to work from a Git checkout, clone the repository with all nested submodules: git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:TheBoutrosLab/SpectroMesa-DDA.git SpectroMesa-DDA cd SpectroMesa-DDA Some submodules use GitHub SSH URLs, so this command requires working GitHub SSH authentication and access to the repositories. To use HTTPS instead, use this alternative clone command: git -c 'url.https://github.com/.insteadOf=git@github.com:' \ clone --recurse-submodules \ https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/SpectroMesa-DDA.git SpectroMesa-DDA cd SpectroMesa-DDA For an existing checkout, initialize any missing submodules from its root: git submodule update --init --recursive When using HTTPS, apply the same command-scoped URL rewrite: git -c 'url.https://github.com/.insteadOf=git@github.com:' \ submodule update --init --recursive The submodules provide the analysis software and configuration included with this pipeline. Keep their versions matched to the pipeline checkout. Check their status with: git submodule status --recursive A leading space indicates the recorded revision is checked out. A leading - means a submodule is not initialized; + means it differs from the recorded revision. Check the container runtime Choose one runtime and use its matching Nextflow profile when launching an analysis: Runtime Check Pipeline profile Docker docker info -profile docker Apptainer apptainer --version -profile apptainer Make sure Docker is running and accessible to your account, or that Apptainer is installed on the machines where the analysis will run. Docker and Apptainer are the documented end-to-end choices. A Singularity profile exists at the top level, but the pinned QC pipeline does not declare it; use Apptainer for that runtime family. For Apptainer, configure persistent caches before launching a run. Use directories you own that are accessible from the execution nodes: export NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$HOME/.cache/nextflow/apptainer" export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$HOME/.apptainer/cache" mkdir -p "$NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR" "$APPTAINER_CACHEDIR" Reuse container images across runs Use shared filesystem paths instead if your home directory is not available on those nodes. Both caches are relevant: some stages use Nextflow-managed images, while others use Apptainer's own image cache. Obtain MSFragger MSFragger is the default search engine. Skip this section if your analysis uses only Comet or Sage. Download MSFragger through its official download instructions under the license appropriate to your use. Keep the extracted distribution in a persistent directory accessible to the analysis tasks. The pipeline requires the path to the JAR, not the containing directory. In your run configuration, set: params.msfragger_executable = '/path/to/MSFragger/MSFragger.jar' Replace the example with the actual filename, which may include a version number. The pipeline does not download this JAR for you. Storage and compute environment Keep the repository, external tools, input data, and work and output directories accessible to the execution environment. Allow working storage for converted mzML files, feature maps, intermediate identifications, and container images. Space requirements depend on the cohort and should not be estimated from final output size alone. Request cluster resources before launching Request a cluster allocation before launching the analysis. The bundled pines and boutroslab_aws profiles specify CPU and memory settings; they do not submit a Slurm job for you. Combine the resource and container profiles, for example -profile pines,apptainer . Verify the setup From the pipeline directory, check: export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow -version test -f main.nf test -f config/template.config test -f external/search-ProteomicMSMS/main.nf test -f external/validate-ProteomicPSM/main.nf test -f external/quantitate-ProteomicLFQ/main.nf test -f external/quantitate-ProteomicTMT/main.nf Confirm the expected Nextflow version, a working container runtime, and readable tool files. If you installed through Git, also check the submodule status as described above. The test commands produce no output when successful and return a nonzero exit status if a file is missing. These checks verify installation prerequisites; they do not run a proteomics analysis or validate all container images. Next, prepare the acquisition table and target-decoy FASTA and create a run configuration from the repository's config/template.config . Preserve its includeConfig statements and final methods.setup() call. Input preparation, scientific settings, and analysis execution are separate from installation. Preview the documentation To work on the documentation locally, install MkDocs in a separate Python environment: python3 -m venv /path/to/mkdocs-env source /path/to/mkdocs-env/bin/activate python -m pip install "mkdocs==1.5.3" mkdocs serve -f /path/to/SpectroMesa-DDA/mkdocs-config.yaml Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ in your browser. Initialize the pipeline submodules first: the site reads their original flowcharts during the build. Use --dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8001 if another documentation server is already using port 8000.

To download the latest release from a terminal, use either wget : wget -O source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/SpectroMesa-DDA/releases/latest/download/source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz or curl : curl -fL -o source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/SpectroMesa-DDA/releases/latest/download/source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz From the directory containing your download, extract it into a folder for the pipeline: mkdir -p SpectroMesa-DDA tar -xzf source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz -C SpectroMesa-DDA --strip-components=1 cd SpectroMesa-DDA You can now continue to check the container runtime .
docs.title: Download a release (recommended)

docs.text: If you prefer to work from a Git checkout, clone the repository with all nested submodules: git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:TheBoutrosLab/SpectroMesa-DDA.git SpectroMesa-DDA cd SpectroMesa-DDA Some submodules use GitHub SSH URLs, so this command requires working GitHub SSH authentication and access to the repositories. To use HTTPS instead, use this alternative clone command: git -c 'url.https://github.com/.insteadOf=git@github.com:' \ clone --recurse-submodules \ https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/SpectroMesa-DDA.git SpectroMesa-DDA cd SpectroMesa-DDA For an existing checkout, initialize any missing submodules from its root: git submodule update --init --recursive When using HTTPS, apply the same command-scoped URL rewrite: git -c 'url.https://github.com/.insteadOf=git@github.com:' \ submodule update --init --recursive The submodules provide the analysis software and configuration included with this pipeline. Keep their versions matched to the pipeline checkout. Check their status with: git submodule status --recursive A leading space indicates the recorded revision is checked out. A leading - means a submodule is not initialized; + means it differs from the recorded revision.
docs.title: Clone with Git (alternative)

docs.text: Choose one runtime and use its matching Nextflow profile when launching an analysis: Runtime Check Pipeline profile Docker docker info -profile docker Apptainer apptainer --version -profile apptainer Make sure Docker is running and accessible to your account, or that Apptainer is installed on the machines where the analysis will run. Docker and Apptainer are the documented end-to-end choices. A Singularity profile exists at the top level, but the pinned QC pipeline does not declare it; use Apptainer for that runtime family. For Apptainer, configure persistent caches before launching a run. Use directories you own that are accessible from the execution nodes: export NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$HOME/.cache/nextflow/apptainer" export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$HOME/.apptainer/cache" mkdir -p "$NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR" "$APPTAINER_CACHEDIR" Reuse container images across runs Use shared filesystem paths instead if your home directory is not available on those nodes. Both caches are relevant: some stages use Nextflow-managed images, while others use Apptainer's own image cache.
docs.title: Check the container runtime

docs.text: MSFragger is the default search engine. Skip this section if your analysis uses only Comet or Sage. Download MSFragger through its official download instructions under the license appropriate to your use. Keep the extracted distribution in a persistent directory accessible to the analysis tasks. The pipeline requires the path to the JAR, not the containing directory. In your run configuration, set: params.msfragger_executable = '/path/to/MSFragger/MSFragger.jar' Replace the example with the actual filename, which may include a version number. The pipeline does not download this JAR for you.
docs.title: Obtain MSFragger

docs.text: Keep the repository, external tools, input data, and work and output directories accessible to the execution environment. Allow working storage for converted mzML files, feature maps, intermediate identifications, and container images. Space requirements depend on the cohort and should not be estimated from final output size alone. Request cluster resources before launching Request a cluster allocation before launching the analysis. The bundled pines and boutroslab_aws profiles specify CPU and memory settings; they do not submit a Slurm job for you. Combine the resource and container profiles, for example -profile pines,apptainer .

docs.text: From the pipeline directory, check: export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow -version test -f main.nf test -f config/template.config test -f external/search-ProteomicMSMS/main.nf test -f external/validate-ProteomicPSM/main.nf test -f external/quantitate-ProteomicLFQ/main.nf test -f external/quantitate-ProteomicTMT/main.nf Confirm the expected Nextflow version, a working container runtime, and readable tool files. If you installed through Git, also check the submodule status as described above. The test commands produce no output when successful and return a nonzero exit status if a file is missing. These checks verify installation prerequisites; they do not run a proteomics analysis or validate all container images. Next, prepare the acquisition table and target-decoy FASTA and create a run configuration from the repository's config/template.config . Preserve its includeConfig statements and final methods.setup() call. Input preparation, scientific settings, and analysis execution are separate from installation.

docs.text: SpectroMesa-DDA overview SpectroMesa-DDA analyzes data-dependent acquisition (DDA) proteomics experiments, from mass spectrometry data to peptide and protein abundances. It supports label-free quantitation (LFQ) and tandem mass tag (TMT) experiments, including fractionated samples, and brings together database searching, identification validation, quantitation, quality control, and optional database assembly. The pipeline uses Nextflow to orchestrate individual tools and analysis steps. Its spectrum-based workflow connects database searching and peptide-spectrum match (PSM) validation to peptide quantitation, protein grouping, and protein quantitation. 1 Workflow Data already in mzML format enter the search stage directly; other supported formats pass through conversion. After identification validation, the workflow follows either the LFQ or TMT branch before returning to shared protein quantitation and quality control. ProteoVault assembly is optional. Major components MS data conversion ProteoWizard msconvert converts supported vendor data to mzML, the format used by downstream stages. OpenMS provides an alternative conversion route for supported open formats, along with peak-picking and indexing options. Conversion is skipped when the input is already mzML. 2 , 3 Database search MSFragger , Comet , and Sage match tandem mass spectra to candidate peptides from a target-decoy protein sequence database. MSFragger is the default search engine; a run can use one engine or combine several. Search results provide the candidate peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) evaluated during validation. 4 , 5 , 6 Identification validation Percolator rescores candidate PSMs to distinguish likely correct matches from decoys. The default route uses OpenMS tools to prepare and process the rescoring results; the optional MSBooster route adds features derived from predicted peptide properties before Percolator rescoring. When multiple search engines are selected, OpenMS ConsensusID combines their identification evidence before the accepted identifications are passed to peptide quantitation. 2 , 7 , 8 Peptide quantitation LFQ uses OpenMS FeatureFinderIdentification to extract chromatographic MS1 features guided by peptide identifications. OpenMS alignment and feature-linking tools bring corresponding features together across samples, producing a quantitative feature map for downstream protein quantitation. 2 TMT uses OpenMS IsobaricAnalyzer to extract reporter-ion intensities and associate them with identified peptides and sample channels. The default workflow quantifies reporter signals; an experimental alternative combines MS1 feature areas with reporter-ion proportions. Both routes produce a quantitative feature map for protein quantitation. 2 Protein inference and quantitation The default route combines identification evidence with iProphet and infers protein groups with ProteinProphet . An alternative uses OpenMS ProteinInference , selected as the ProteinInferencer route. OpenMS ProteinQuantifier then summarizes peptide evidence into peptide and protein abundance tables using the selected protein groups. 2 , 9 , 10 Quality control The DDA QC pipeline uses pyOpenMS and dedicated summary scripts to examine acquisition data, search results, validated identifications, protein groups, and quantitative outputs. It produces cohort QC tables and interactive MS1 plots to help inspect signal quality and variation across samples or TMT plexes. 2 Results database ProteoVault optionally assembles the completed identification, quantitation, and QC results into a validated DuckDB database. This provides a common entry point for querying the cohort while retaining the individual pipeline outputs. The generated DuckDB database can be imported and analyzed in R using ProteoVaultR . References Nextflow: Di Tommaso P et al. (2017). Nextflow enables reproducible computational workflows. Nature Biotechnology . doi:10.1038/nbt.3820 . OpenMS: Pfeuffer J et al. (2024). OpenMS 3 enables reproducible analysis of large-scale mass spectrometry data. Nature Methods . doi:10.1038/s41592-024-02197-7 . ProteoWizard: Kessner D et al. (2008). ProteoWizard: open source software for rapid proteomics tools development. Bioinformatics . doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btn323 . MSFragger: Kong AT et al. (2017). MSFragger: ultrafast and comprehensive peptide identification in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. Nature Methods . doi:10.1038/nmeth.4256 . Comet: Eng JK, Jahan TA, Hoopmann MR (2013). Comet: an open-source MS/MS sequence database search tool. Proteomics . doi:10.1002/pmic.201200439 . Sage: Lazear MR (2023). Sage: an open-source tool for fast proteomics searching and quantification at scale. Journal of Proteome Research . doi:10.1021/acs.jproteome.3c00486 . Percolator: Käll L et al. (2007). Semi-supervised learning for peptide identification from shotgun proteomics datasets. Nature Methods . doi:10.1038/nmeth1113 . MSBooster: Yang KL et al. (2023). MSBooster: improving peptide identification rates using deep learning-based features. Nature Communications . doi:10.1038/s41467-023-40129-9 . iProphet: Shteynberg D et al. docs.text: Understanding results Start with the final protein and peptide abundance tables , then review the QC summaries before comparing samples. If database assembly is enabled, ProteoVault provides a single DuckDB database that can be loaded and analyzed in R with ProteoVaultR . Where results are written The output_dir and dataset_id in your run configuration determine the result location: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DDA-<version>/ ├── <dataset_id>.proteovault.duckdb └── <dataset_id>/ ├── main_workflow/ │ ├── convert-MSData-<version>/ # when conversion is needed │ ├── search-ProteomicMSMS-<version>/ │ ├── validate-ProteomicPSM-<version>/ │ ├── quantitate-ProteomicLFQ-<version>/ # LFQ analyses │ ├── quantitate-ProteomicTMT-<version>/ # TMT analyses │ ├── quantitate-ProteomicProtein-<version>/ │ ├── qc-ProteomicDDA-<version>/ │ └── manifests/ └── log-SpectroMesa-DDA-<version>-<timestamp>/ Only the selected quantitation branch is present. The database is created when run_proteovault is true, which is the default. Version placeholders refer to the software used for the run, not necessarily the latest release. Protein and peptide abundance tables The final tables are under: main_workflow/quantitate-ProteomicProtein-<version>/ <dataset_id>/OpenMS-<version>/output/ <dataset_id>_ProteinQuantifier_protein.csv <dataset_id>_ProteinQuantifier_peptide.csv The protein table summarizes peptide evidence according to the selected protein groups. The peptide table provides the corresponding peptide-level quantities; its row and column detail depends on charge and fraction settings. Inspect the exported identifiers and headers before treating a protein group as a single protein or gene. The CSV files are tab-delimited With the default export settings, ProteinQuantifier writes tab-separated data despite the .csv extension. Read them with a tab-delimited reader or through ProteoVaultR, rather than assuming commas separate columns. For LFQ , abundance columns identify sample assays. By default, fractions within each assay are summed and charge states are combined. Technical replicates with separate sample identifiers remain separate assays. For TMT , abundance columns identify plex/channel assays, with channel descriptions where available. The default scan-based workflow measures reporter-ion signal. The experimental feature-based route apportions MS1 feature area using reporter proportions. MAD normalization can produce quasi-intensities or log2 ratios depending on MADNormalizer.quasi_intensity ; retain the run configuration so the values can be interpreted correctly. Column relabeling preserves the numeric values and stops if an assay cannot be matched unambiguously. It does not merge identically named biological samples across different TMT channels. Detailed peptide tables can retain file, fraction, and charge information, so do not assume they have the same layout as the protein table. Protein groups and identification confidence The protein quantitation directory also contains the grouping result: Grouping route File What it represents ProteinProphet <dataset_id>_ProteinProphet.protXML Raw grouping result before the pipeline's probability filtering. ProteinProphet <dataset_id>_ProteinProphet_filtered.idXML Groups supplied to ProteinQuantifier, with zero-probability parent groups removed. ProteinInferencer <dataset_id>_IDConflictResolver.consensusXML Inferred groups and quantified features after any enabled protein FDR filtering and identification conflict resolution. PSM and protein confidence are different The default validation threshold is a PSM q-value of 0.01 . The default ProteinProphet route does not apply a 1% protein q-value filter. In the ProteinInferencer route, protein FDR calculation and filtering are both off by default. See Protein grouping and quantitation for the settings that control this. Search and validation directories retain the identification evidence. Filtered idXML files describe accepted PSMs for each sample or TMT plex. Unfiltered PEP-scored idXML files retain evidence used for cohort ProteinProphet grouping and should not be interpreted as an accepted-identification list. For multiple search engines, use the final consensus identifications for combined counts rather than summing the per-engine filtered files. Quantitation details The LFQ or TMT directory contains the feature maps used for protein quantitation. The final *_IDConflictResolver.consensusXML resolves conflicting peptide assignments before the protein step. These files are useful for investigating feature-level quantities and sample mapping. TMT also publishes a dataset peptide table and, for feature-based quantitation, <dataset_id>_LinkedFeatures.tsv . The linked table records the input fraction_id , plex_id , reporter label, and sample description. In the merged TMT peptide CSV, the design fraction does not necessarily equal the input acquisition's fraction_id ; use the linked table when tracing feature-based results back to input fractions. docs.text: Running the tests The integration tests run SpectroMesa-DDA on small reference datasets to check that the analysis completes in your computing environment. You will need the installed pipeline, the public test data, the required search software, and UCLA NFTest . Start with one case before trying the other acquisition and quantitation routes. Install the test tools Complete the pipeline installation , including its submodules, Java, Nextflow, and the container runtime you will use. The test launcher also needs Python 3.8 or newer and UCLA NFTest ( uclahs-cds/tool-NFTest ) . You can keep the Python tools in a dedicated environment: python3 -m venv "$HOME/.venvs/spectromesa-tests" source "$HOME/.venvs/spectromesa-tests/bin/activate" python3 -m pip install \ "git+https://github.com/uclahs-cds/tool-NFTest.git" \ PyYAML python-dotenv python3 -m nftest --help If your NFTest version imports pkg_resources , install setuptools<81 in this environment. Activate this environment whenever you run a test, including inside a cluster job. The launcher uses NFTest from the same Python environment as python3 . Use the tested Nextflow settings: export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 Download the public test data The Boutros Lab public S3 location is s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/ . DDA fixtures are under spectromesa/ecoli_lfq/ , spectromesa/ecoli_tmt/ , and spectromesa/database/ . Install the AWS CLI , then choose a persistent directory: export TEST_DATA_DIR=/path/to/test/data mkdir -p "$TEST_DATA_DIR" aws s3 sync --no-sign-request \ s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/spectromesa/database/ \ "$TEST_DATA_DIR/database/" aws s3 sync --no-sign-request \ s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/spectromesa/ecoli_lfq/mzML/ \ "$TEST_DATA_DIR/ecoli_lfq/mzML/" aws s3 sync --no-sign-request \ s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/spectromesa/ecoli_tmt/mzML/ \ "$TEST_DATA_DIR/ecoli_tmt/mzML/" For the RAW conversion case, also download: aws s3 sync --no-sign-request \ s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/spectromesa/ecoli_tmt/Raw/ \ "$TEST_DATA_DIR/ecoli_tmt/Raw/" --no-sign-request allows these public downloads without AWS credentials. Keep the directory names and filenames intact. The repository supplies the test acquisition and channel CSVs, so you do not need to construct them manually. Match the test database Update the older FASTA path in the selected test The checked-in test configurations currently name an older FASTA that is not in the public fixture listing. Before running a case with the public download, update its database path and accession markers together. The available FASTA below uses DECOY_ decoys and contam_ contaminants. In the selected test/<case>/test.config , use: params { decoy_database = "${TEST_DATA_DIR}/database/UP000000625_83333-FragPipe/2026-11-12-decoys-contam-input.fasta.fas" decoy_string = 'DECOY_' decoy_position = 'prefix' contam_string = 'contam_' contam_position = 'prefix' } Edit the existing values before methods.setup() ; preserve the rest of the test's scientific settings. The shared database markers are propagated to search, validation, and protein quantitation. Changing the FASTA changes the scientific test input, so record the database used when comparing runs. The E. coli TMT fixture is described as a protein-spike experiment: verify that your sequence set contains any spike proteins you intend to evaluate; a workflow completion test is not a benchmark of their recovery. Supply MSFragger separately For MSFragger cases, obtain the licensed distribution as described in Installation , and place MSFragger-4.4.1.jar directly under TEST_DATA_DIR , or update the selected test's JAR path. The public bucket download does not supply this JAR. The Sage LFQ case does not need MSFragger. Configure the test environment Unlike ordinary analyses, the test launcher is run from the repository root because it reads the repository's nftest.yml . Copy .env-template to .env if you have not already configured it: cd /path/to/SpectroMesa-DDA cp .env-template .env Edit .env with your paths and execution environment: NXF_VER=24.10.6 NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 TEST_DATA_DIR=/path/to/test/data NFT_RUN_ROOT=/scratch/your_user/spectromesa-dda-tests NFT_CLUSTER=pines NFT_CLUSTER Execution environment Run location pines Apptainer with the 64 CPU, 500 GB resource plan NFT_RUN_ROOT boutroslab_aws Docker with the 32 CPU, 128 GB resource plan; requires SLURM_JOB_ID NFT_RUN_ROOT/SLURM_JOB_ID Unset or empty Docker with the AWS resource plan NFT_RUN_ROOT Request an appropriate compute allocation first. These resource plans do not submit a cluster job. Relative NFT_RUN_ROOT values resolve from the repository root; if unset, the root defaults to the repository. For Apptainer, set persistent caches as described in Installation . Run a test case Activate the Python environment containing UCLA NFTest and run one case from the repository root: python3 test/run-nftest.py test_integration_MSFragger_LFQ_Protein The current cases are: Case Coverage ProteoVault test_integration_MSFragger_LFQ_Protein MSFragger, two fractions per LFQ sample, ProteinProphet, QC Disabled in the test configuration test_integration_Sage_LFQ_Protein Sage on the same fractionated LFQ fixture, ProteinProphet, QC Enabled test_integration_MSFragger_TMT_Protein MSFragger, three fractions per TMT plex, experimental feature-based TMT with MAD normalization, ProteinProphet, QC Disabled in the test configuration test_integration_MSFragger_TMT_Reindexed Two fractions per TMT plex, spectrum reindexing, scan-based TMT, ProteinProphet, QC Enabled test_integration_MSFragger_TMT_RAW RAW conversion, one acquisition per TMT plex, scan-based TMT, ProteinProphet, QC Enabled Use the case name as the launcher's argument. Start with one case and resolve its setup errors before running the full set. The supplied cases exercise workflow completion and file handoffs; nftest.yml does not define numerical assertions for biological results. Inspect the run Results are written under <run-root>/<test-case>/ ; temporary work is under <run-root>/.nftest-temp/<12-character case ID>/ . The launcher retains temporary files to help investigate failures. Check the final exit status, logs, expected quantitative outputs, and QC summaries. A successful setup check or a partially populated output directory is not evidence that the integration test completed. The test CSVs expand TEST_DATA_DIR through the supplied launcher configuration. Ordinary analysis CSVs should contain actual paths as described in Preparing inputs . Keep the test work directories while investigating a failure and review the resume limitations before relaunching.

docs.text: Label-free quantitation OpenMS FeatureFinderIdentification extracts MS1 peptide features guided by accepted identifications. Alignment and feature linking then connect corresponding features across samples. Open the original flowchart at full size . How it works Match each sample's validated identifications to its acquisition fractions. Extract and quantify identification-guided chromatographic features with FFId. docs.text: Protein grouping and quantitation ProteinProphet or OpenMS ProteinInference assigns protein groups, and OpenMS ProteinQuantifier summarizes the quantified peptide evidence into protein and peptide abundance tables. Open the original flowchart at full size . How it works Receive the final LFQ or TMT consensusXML containing quantitative features. With the default ProteinProphet route, convert the unfiltered PEP-scored identifications to pepXML, repair supported enzyme-terminus annotations, combine the evidence with iProphet, and infer groups with ProteinProphet. Remove zero-probability parent groups and supply the resulting protein groups to ProteinQuantifier. Alternatively, use ProteinInferencer to infer groups directly in the consensusXML, optionally calculate and filter protein FDR, and resolve identification conflicts. Quantify peptide and protein abundances, then label columns using the feature map's experimental design and channel descriptions. Inputs and outputs All inputs are supplied automatically: the cohort quantitative feature map, unfiltered PEP-scored idXML manifest, target-decoy FASTA, and shared identifiers. ProteinProphet combines evidence across the cohort rather than performing independent grouping for each sample. Final outputs are <dataset_id>_ProteinQuantifier_protein.csv and <dataset_id>_ProteinQuantifier_peptide.csv . The ProteinProphet route also publishes raw protXML and the filtered idXML used for quantitation. The ProteinInferencer route retains its groups in the final IDConflictResolver.consensusXML . See Understanding results for paths and table interpretation. A configured cutoff does not enable filtering protein_fdr_cutoff is 0.01 , but both FDR switches are false by default. Protein FDR filtering applies only in the ProteinInferencer route when protein_inference_protein_fdr and filter_protein_fdr are both true. The default ProteinProphet route removes zero-probability groups and does not apply this q-value cutoff. By default, ProteinQuantifier combines charge states and sums fractions within each assay. protein_quantifier_best_charge = true selects one charge per modified peptide; protein_quantifier_fractions_aggregate = 'best' selects the best fraction per peptide and fraction group. These choices affect quantities and the detailed peptide table layout. Parameter reference Use the quantitate_ProteomicProtein block inside params . docs.text: Results database ProteoVault combines completed DDA results into a validated DuckDB database. It provides a common entry point for querying identifications, quantitative results, sequence information, and QC. How it works Collect the completed search, validation, LFQ or TMT, protein quantitation, and QC outputs. Import the acquisition manifest and target-decoy FASTA; TMT also supplies the channel CSV and reporter type. Build the database using ProteoVault's DDA importer and validate it before publishing. Inputs and outputs All inputs are supplied automatically. The output is <dataset_id>.proteovault.duckdb under <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DDA-<version>/ , above the dataset's analysis directory. The individual analysis outputs remain available alongside the database. Load and analyze the database in R using ProteoVaultR . Source paths stored in the database refer to the build work directory; use proteovault update-paths when you need to reconnect those links after moving the results. See the ProteoVault CLI guide . Parameter reference These are shared settings directly inside params , without a separate block: Parameter Type Default Meaning run_proteovault Boolean true Already enabled. Set false to finish after QC without assembling the database. proteovault_version Text 0.2.5 ProteoVault image version. Check importer compatibility before changing it. docker_image_proteovault Text ghcr.io/theboutroslab/proteovault:0.2.5 Container image used to build and validate the database. When the default image is still selected, changing proteovault_version updates its image tag during setup. An explicitly chosen alternative image takes precedence. This setting controls only database assembly, not the upstream analysis. Related steps Understanding results · Quality control · Shared parameters

docs.text: Quality control The QC pipeline summarizes acquisitions, identifications, protein groups, and abundance tables. Interactive MS1 maps help you inspect acquisition signal alongside those summaries. Open the original flowchart at full size . How it works Summarize each mzML fraction's scans, timing, and signal, and select peaks for an interactive MS1 map. Summarize unfiltered search results, final filtered identifications, and available PSM-feature files. Summarize the cohort protein groups used for quantitation. Match protein and peptide abundance columns to LFQ samples or TMT plex/channels, then produce a combined metric table. Inputs and outputs SpectroMesa-DDA supplies the manifests, inference result, abundance tables, and TMT channel CSV. If search reindexing is enabled, QC uses those same reindexed mzML files. No separate QC input list is needed. Outputs include <dataset_id>_QC_metrics.tsv , per-stage summaries, and per-fraction *_MS1_landscape.html plots. The results guide explains their locations and the shared 12-column metric schema. QC reports the existing results; it does not change identification thresholds or quantities. The default pyOpenMS image is 3.5.0, and the MultiQC image supplies Plotly for the offline plots. This pipeline supports Docker and Apptainer profiles. Resolve ambiguous assay labels If an abundance header cannot be matched unambiguously, set assay_mapping_csv to a CSV with level,abundance_column,sample_name,fraction_id,reporter_channel,group . level is protein or peptide ; abundance_column must exactly match the original table header. Leave fraction_id empty for an assay spanning fractions and use the channel description as group for TMT. The pipeline fails on ambiguous mappings instead of guessing. Parameter reference Use the qc_ProteomicDDA block inside params . Defaults below describe this step as launched by SpectroMesa-DDA. “Not set; tool default” means no override is passed. docs.text: Database search MSFragger , Comet , and Sage match tandem mass spectra to peptides in your target-decoy FASTA. MSFragger is selected by default; you can combine engines to contribute complementary identification evidence. How it works Optionally reindex mzML spectra so native IDs are unique across a sample's fractions. This is off by default in SpectroMesa-DDA. Search each acquisition with every selected engine through its OpenMS adapter. Match peptides to proteins with PeptideIndexer and retain target/decoy labels. Merge fractions into one unfiltered idXML per sample and engine for validation . Inputs and outputs Inputs are the prepared mzML acquisitions, the shared target-decoy FASTA, and the MSFragger JAR when that engine is used. SpectroMesa-DDA supplies their paths. Outputs include per-acquisition search results and merged sample/engine idXML files. They are candidate identifications, before the downstream q-value filtering. Files sharing sample_name contribute to the same validation unit. For TMT, that unit is a plex; its reporter channels identify biological samples later. See Preparing inputs . Parameter reference Use the search_ProteomicMSMS block. Engine settings below include the actual search template used by this metapipeline. For example, MSFragger uses a 30 ppm precursor tolerance on either side and a 0.02 Da fragment tolerance unless overridden. Review each engine's digestion and modification settings when combining searches. Configure TMT labels in the search plex_type selects reporter-ion quantitation and does not set search modifications. Add the label chemistry to each selected engine as described in Configuring an analysis . Use the search_ProteomicMSMS block inside params . docs.text: TMT quantitation OpenMS IsobaricAnalyzer extracts TMT reporter signals and associates them with peptide identifications and channel descriptions. The default workflow measures reporter-ion intensities; an experimental alternative apportions MS1 feature areas to reporter channels. Open the original flowchart at full size . How it works Group acquisition fractions by TMT plex and map the channels from your channel CSV. Extract reporter ions with IsobaricAnalyzer, using the selected label set and isotope-correction options. For scan_based , attach peptide identifications to reporter features and merge the plex maps. For feature_based , extract MS1 features with FFId, align corresponding fractions across plexes, and apportion each feature's area using its matched reporter-ion proportions. Link features and combine the fraction maps. Apply the selected normalization, resolve competing identifications, and export the final consensusXML and peptide table for protein quantitation . Inputs and outputs The acquisition and identification manifests are supplied automatically. Provide the channel CSV through the shared channel_csv setting and choose plex_type to match the labels. The same reporter type is used throughout a run. Both routes publish <dataset_id>_IDConflictResolver.consensusXML and <dataset_id>_ProteinQuantifier_peptide.csv . The feature-based route also writes <dataset_id>_LinkedFeatures.tsv , retaining the original fraction, plex, and channel identifiers. MAD normalization writes scaling information and a normalized feature map. Optional intermediate maps and per-run diagnostics are controlled by save_intermediate_files . Normalization and workflow choices Normalization is already enabled. SpectroMesa-DDA launches a template that selects mad , using MSPtools MADNormalizer on the merged dataset. This overrides the standalone pipeline's openms default. The alternative openms method uses IsobaricAnalyzer's median-ratio normalization and a channel labeled reference in each plex. MAD uses a physical reference by default; MADNormalizer.virtual_reference = true derives a reference from reporter intensities instead. MAD writes reference-scaled quasi-intensities by default. Setting MADNormalizer.quasi_intensity = false writes normalized log2 ratios. Zero then represents equality to the reference, so the workflow skips its all-zero-plex missingness cleanup for that output mode. With quasi-intensity or OpenMS-normalized output, the cleanup distinguishes unobserved plexes from measured quantities. Feature-based TMT requires a deliberate choice tmt_workflow defaults to scan_based . The feature_based route is experimental and requires matching fraction IDs across plexes. If normalization is enabled, keep tmt_normalization_method = 'mad' ; OpenMS normalization is incompatible with feature-based quantitation. Bridge scaling is off by default. For feature-based MAD quasi-intensities, MADNormalizer.bridge_scale = true scales plexes using their median valid reference areas. With a physical reference, use a common reference sample across plexes. Virtual-reference bridge scaling additionally requires MADNormalizer.allow_virtual_bridge = true and assumes comparable overall composition. docs.text: PSM validation Percolator rescores candidate PSMs, and OpenMS estimates q-values and filters the identifications. The default route uses OpenMS PercolatorAdapter; MSBooster can add predicted-property features before rescoring. Open the original flowchart at full size . How it works Check peptide-to-protein associations and target/decoy labels against the shared FASTA. Extract PSM features and run Percolator using the selected openms or msbooster route. Estimate sample-level PSM q-values and filter at 0.01 by default. When multiple search engines are selected, combine their evidence with ConsensusID. Fractionated input is handled automatically. Supply accepted identifications to peptide quantitation and unfiltered PEP-scored identifications to the later protein grouping step . Inputs and outputs SpectroMesa-DDA generates the search-result and mzML manifests and provides the shared FASTA. Outputs include per-engine filtered idXML, optional multi-engine consensus idXML, unfiltered PEP-scored idXML, and PSM-feature files used by QC. Protein grouping for this DDA workflow happens after LFQ or TMT quantitation. The standalone validation pipeline's library-generation routes are not used here. Keep Percolator enabled for ProteinProphet run_percolator already defaults to true . ProteinProphet requires its PEP-scored identification files. The filter_psm_score_peptide setting is passed as a PSM score threshold, despite its historical name; with default q-value scoring, 0.01 means a 1% PSM threshold. docs.title: validate-ProteomicPSM

docs.text: Percolator rescores candidate PSMs, and OpenMS estimates q-values and filters the identifications. The default route uses OpenMS PercolatorAdapter; MSBooster can add predicted-property features before rescoring. Open the original flowchart at full size .
docs.title: PSM validation

docs.text: Check peptide-to-protein associations and target/decoy labels against the shared FASTA. Extract PSM features and run Percolator using the selected openms or msbooster route. Estimate sample-level PSM q-values and filter at 0.01 by default. When multiple search engines are selected, combine their evidence with ConsensusID. Fractionated input is handled automatically. Supply accepted identifications to peptide quantitation and unfiltered PEP-scored identifications to the later protein grouping step .
docs.title: How it works

docs.text: SpectroMesa-DDA generates the search-result and mzML manifests and provides the shared FASTA. Outputs include per-engine filtered idXML, optional multi-engine consensus idXML, unfiltered PEP-scored idXML, and PSM-feature files used by QC. Protein grouping for this DDA workflow happens after LFQ or TMT quantitation. The standalone validation pipeline's library-generation routes are not used here. Keep Percolator enabled for ProteinProphet run_percolator already defaults to true . ProteinProphet requires its PEP-scored identification files. The filter_psm_score_peptide setting is passed as a PSM score threshold, despite its historical name; with default q-value scoring, 0.01 means a 1% PSM threshold.
